title: Misinformation, Conspiracies & AI Persuasion
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

nodes.title: What claim means

A statement presented as something that could be true or false.

One important limit: Before judging support, identify exactly what outcome the claim is about.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Theo shares a social-media claim that a common household substance prevents infection. Lila asks where the information came from.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Hasher et al. (1977), frequency and validity; Fazio et al. (2015), knowledge and illusory truth.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.

nodes.scenario: Theo shares a social-media claim that a common household substance prevents infection. Lila asks where the information came from.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I've seen that claim everywhere this week. It must have something behind it.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Are the posts coming from different studies or copying the same video?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I didn't check. It was shared by several accounts I recognise.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Do any of the posts link to an actual controlled study?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.
checks.counterexample: Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.
nodes.sources: Hasher et al. (1977), frequency and validity; Fazio et al. (2015), knowledge and illusory truth.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Repeated exposure can increase perceived truth even when the underlying evidence has not improved. Recognition is being used as a shortcut for evidential reliability.

Another possibility: The claim could still be true. Repetition alone neither establishes nor refutes the proposition; it is independent testing that changes its evidential status.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Trace the earliest verifiable source, then check whether the method and findings support the specific claim being repeated. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.
nodes.sources: Hasher et al. (1977), frequency and validity; Fazio et al. (2015), knowledge and illusory truth.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Trace the earliest verifiable source, then check whether the method and findings support the specific claim being repeated.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: The earliest source turns out to be an advertisement quoting a study that tested a different substance in laboratory conditions, not a preventive treatment in humans.
nodes.sources: Hasher et al. (1977), frequency and validity; Fazio et al. (2015), knowledge and illusory truth.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The source trail undermines the health claim as presented. The original evidence does not establish the effect being asserted by the posts.
nodes.counterexample: Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.
nodes.sources: Hasher et al. (1977), frequency and validity; Fazio et al. (2015), knowledge and illusory truth.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: I've seen it everywhere
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of familiarity mistaken for truth.

nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Theo may trust the accounts repeating the claim because they have previously shared accurate information.
options.feedback: Source reputation could affect confidence, though reposting the same claim does not provide independent evidence.

options.label: Ivo may be mistaking repetition of one claim for several independent confirmations.
Several local observers may independently have found evidence of the same problem.
The claim may have originated in a genuine study that has been overextended in social posts.
options.feedback: This is worth checking; the original method must support the specific proposed benefit.

options.label: Theo may be treating popularity as a rough proxy for scrutiny, assuming that someone else must have checked it.
options.feedback: Widespread sharing can create that impression, but it does not establish that checking occurred.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Ivo may be mistaking repetition of one claim for several independent confirmations. Several local observers may independently have found evidence of the same problem. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: A repeated claim can still be true. Familiarity is not evidence for truth or falsity by itself.

checks.prompt: You are Ivo. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.reply: Do you know where it originally came from?
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.reply: Did it link to a water test?
options.consequence: Independent help can be appropriate when direct discussion fails or safety requires it; timing matters.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A political claim appears in dozens of posts that all reproduce the same unattributed screenshot. Readers mistake the number of reposts for corroboration.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Repeated exposure can increase perceived truth even when the underlying evidence has not improved. Recognition is being used as a shortcut for evidential reliability.

Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Hasher et al. (1977), frequency and validity; Fazio et al. (2015), knowledge and illusory truth.

glossary.definition: A statement presented as something that could be true or false.
glossary.example: A video says a household substance prevents a particular infection.
glossary.limit: Before judging support, identify exactly what outcome the claim is about.

glossary.definition: Information gathered in a way that can help test whether a claim is supported.
glossary.example: A controlled human study measures whether the proposed intervention actually works.
glossary.limit: A cited laboratory result might not justify a health claim about people.

glossary.definition: New support that does not simply copy the same original source.
glossary.example: Several research teams separately test the same question with suitable methods.
glossary.limit: Fifteen reposts of one video are still one unverified source.

glossary.definition: A tendency for repeated statements to feel more believable because they become easier to recognise.
glossary.example: A headline seems credible after appearing in several feeds over the same week.
glossary.limit: Familiarity does not prove accuracy, and repetition does not mean the statement is necessarily false.
